opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the thing that struck me first wasn't any single answer. It was the way it worked through a problem. I gave it some fairly gnarly questions, the kind where a normal model would confidently give you something that sounds right and falls apart when you poke it. o1 Pro would slow down, try an approach, notice it wasn't working, and backtrack. That felt qualitatively different. It was less like autocomplete and more like watching someone actually reason.

On the practical side, I threw some research-style problems at it, things like debugging subtle issues in experiment code or thinking through why an interpretability result might be an artifact rather than a real finding. It caught things I'd expect a sharp collaborator to catch. It didn't just answer the question I asked. Sometimes it pushed back on the framing, and that's when I thought, okay, this is a real step change.

For me there was a second layer, because of what we work on. When you see a model doing that kind of extended reasoning, the obvious next question is what's actually going on inside. Is the chain of thought you see a faithful picture of the computation, or a plausible story laid on top of it? As these systems get more capable and we lean on them for harder, higher-stakes work, being able to see into that process stops being academic. So o1 Pro impressed me as a user, and it also made the case for interpretability feel a lot more urgent.

r001.rationale: The response describes o1 Pro handling both experiment-code debugging and interpretability questions, but does not say that its ability to transfer understanding across domains was what impressed Eric Ho.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that got me was that it felt like the first time a model would actually sit with a problem instead of just reacting to it. We threw a hard case at it, one of those messy reasoning problems where every previous model would confidently sprint off in the wrong direction, and o1 Pro just took its time. You'd watch the thinking unfold and it would backtrack, catch its own mistake, try a different angle. That reflex of "wait, let me check that" was something I hadn't seen behave reliably before.

The second thing was consistency. A lot of models can get a hard problem right once if you reroll enough times. What impressed me with o1 Pro was that it got it right the fifth time too. For anyone trying to build on top of these systems, that reliability matters way more than a single dazzling demo.

And then there was this moment where I asked it something where I already knew the answer was subtle, and instead of telling me what I wanted to hear, it pushed back and explained why my framing was slightly off. It was right. That's when I thought, okay, this isn't just a faster autocomplete. The compute at test time was actually buying real reasoning.

r001.rationale: The response highlights careful reasoning, consistency, and correcting the user's framing, but does not say that o1 Pro transfers understanding across domains.

astra-6.text: What impressed me was how much less I had to steer it. With other models, you often get a promising first answer, but then you’re pointing out gaps and helping it work through them. With o1 Pro, it felt like more of that work was happening before it came back to me. The exciting part wasn’t just getting a better answer—it was feeling like I could hand over a harder problem and spend less time managing the process.

sol-6.1.text: What impressed me was how well it could stay with a difficult problem. With earlier models, I’d often get a plausible first answer, but then I’d have to guide them through the tricky parts. With o1 Pro, it felt like it was doing more of that work itself—checking assumptions, considering alternatives, and coming back with something more complete. I still needed to verify the answer, but I could hand it a more substantial piece of work.

r001.rationale: The response says o1 Pro could work through difficult problems more independently, but does not mention transferring understanding across domains.
